title: Check if Two String Arrays are Equivalent
description:
# Check if Two String Arrays are Equivalent

Given two string arrays `word1` and `word2`, return `true` if they represent the same final string, and return `false` otherwise.

A string array represents a string by concatenating all of its elements from left to right. For example, `["ab", "c"]` represents `"abc"`.

The split points inside the arrays do not matter. Only the final concatenated character sequence matters.

## Example 1

**Input**
word1 = ["ab", "c"], word2 = ["a", "bc"]

**Output**
true

**Explanation**
`word1` represents `"ab" + "c" = "abc"`.
`word2` represents `"a" + "bc" = "abc"`.
Both arrays represent the same string.

## Example 2

**Input**
word1 = ["a", "cb"], word2 = ["ab", "c"]

**Output**
false

**Explanation**
`word1` represents `"acb"`, while `word2` represents `"abc"`.

## Example 3

**Input**
word1 = ["abc", "d", "defg"], word2 = ["abcddefg"]

**Output**
true

## Constraints

* `1 <= word1.length, word2.length <= 1000`
* `1 <= word1[i].length, word2[i].length <= 1000`
* `1 <= sum(word1[i].length), sum(word2[i].length) <= 1000`
* `word1[i]` and `word2[i]` consist of lowercase English letters.

solutions.name: Concatenate And Compare
solutions.description:
## Approach
Build the full string represented by each array, then compare the two final strings with `equals`.

## Key Insight
This is the direct definition of equivalence: two arrays are equivalent exactly when their concatenations are identical. It is a good baseline because it is short and hard to get wrong.

## Complexity Analysis
Let `n` be the total number of characters across both arrays. Building the two strings and comparing them costs O(n) time. The two built strings store up to O(n) characters, so the extra space complexity is O(n).

solutions.name: Two Pointers Across Chunks
solutions.description:
## Approach
Compare the represented strings without building them. Keep a word index and a character index for each array, and advance each side one character at a time.

## Key Insight
The arrays are different chunkings of a character stream. When a character index reaches the end of its current chunk, move to the next chunk and reset the character index to zero.

## Complexity Analysis
Every character is read once, so the time complexity is O(n). The algorithm stores only four indices and a few temporaries, so the space complexity is O(1).

solutions.name: Chunk Character Stream
solutions.description:
## Approach
Wrap each string array in a small `CharStream` helper. The main method compares the next character from each stream until one stream ends or a mismatch appears.

## Key Insight
The helper separates two concerns: the main algorithm asks whether two streams are equal, while `CharStream` owns the boundary logic for moving from one chunk to the next.

## Complexity Analysis
Each call to `next` consumes exactly one character, so the total time complexity is O(n). Each stream stores only two indices and a reference to the array, so the extra space complexity is O(1).

solutions.name: Character Queues
solutions.description:
## Approach
Expand each array into a queue of characters, then remove characters from both queues in lockstep. If a removed pair differs, return `false`; otherwise both queues must become empty together.

## Key Insight
A queue makes the represented string order explicit while still teaching the idea of comparing two streams from the front. It is less memory efficient than the pointer solution, but it is a useful stepping stone for learners.

## Complexity Analysis
Each character is enqueued once and dequeued once, so the time complexity is O(n). The queues store the represented strings as characters, so the extra space complexity is O(n).
